items.prompt: Which chamber of the heart pumps oxygen-rich blood out into the aorta and around the body?

options.label: Right ventricle
Left atrium
Left ventricle
Right atrium

rubric: The left ventricle pushes oxygenated blood into the aorta for the systemic circulation.
The right ventricle is a common wrong pick because it is also a large pumping chamber, but it sends blood to the lungs.

items.prompt: Which hormone, released by the pancreas, lowers blood glucose by helping cells take up sugar?

options.label: Cortisol
Adrenaline
Glucagon
Insulin

rubric: Insulin from pancreatic beta cells lowers blood glucose.
Glucagon is also made in the pancreas but raises blood glucose.

items.prompt: What is the basic functional cell of the nervous system that carries electrical signals?

options.label: Nephron
Neuron
Sarcomere
Alveolus

rubric: Neurons conduct nerve impulses.
Nephrons, alveoli and sarcomeres are units of the kidney, lung and muscle respectively.

items.prompt: In which structures of the lungs does gas exchange between air and blood take place?

options.label: Alveoli
Trachea
Pleura
Bronchi

rubric: Alveoli are thin-walled air sacs surrounded by capillaries where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.
Bronchi and trachea only conduct air; the pleura is a membrane around the lungs.

items.prompt: Which tissue connects one bone to another bone at a joint?

options.label: Ligament
Fascia
Cartilage
Tendon

rubric: Ligaments join bone to bone.
Tendons are often confused with them but join muscle to bone.

items.prompt: Which of the following are parts of the central nervous system? Select all that apply.

options.label: Vagus nerve
Brain
Sciatic nerve
Spinal cord

rubric: The CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord.
Sciatic and vagus nerves are peripheral nerves.

items.prompt: A first-aid trainer asks you to check a casualty's pulse at the wrist. You place two fingers on the thumb side of the inner wrist. Which artery are you feeling?

options.label: Carotid artery
Aorta
Radial artery
Femoral artery

rubric: The radial pulse is felt at the thumb side of the wrist.
Carotid (neck) and femoral (groin) are other pulse sites that learners mix up.

items.prompt: Why do arteries have thick, elastic walls compared with veins?

options.label: They withstand high-pressure surges from the heart and recoil to keep blood moving
They need to absorb nutrients from blood, so thick walls give a larger surface
They must store most of the body's blood volume, so the walls stretch to hold large amounts
They prevent backflow of blood, so the thick walls close tightly between heartbeats

rubric: Arteries receive blood at high pressure and their elastic walls stretch and recoil.
Storing volume describes veins; backflow prevention is the job of valves.

items.prompt: What best describes a negative feedback loop in the body?

options.label: A response that only happens when the body is ill, so the variable is reset by disease
A response that amplifies a change, pushing the variable further from its set point
A response that reverses a change, bringing the variable back toward its set point
A response that stops all activity in an organ, so the variable stays fixed forever

rubric: Negative feedback opposes change to maintain homeostasis.
Amplifying a change is positive feedback, a common mix-up.

items.prompt: When the biceps brachii contracts and shortens, what happens at the elbow joint?

options.label: The elbow flexes and the forearm moves toward the upper arm
The elbow locks and the forearm stays still
The elbow extends and the forearm straightens
The elbow rotates and the forearm turns sideways

rubric: The biceps flexes the elbow by pulling the forearm toward the upper arm.
Extension is performed by the triceps, the opposing muscle.

items.prompt: The thyroid gland releases hormones into the blood to control metabolic rate. To which body system does it belong?

options.label: Lymphatic system
Digestive system
Endocrine system
Nervous system

rubric: Glands that secrete hormones into the blood form the endocrine system.
The thyroid sits in the neck, but it is not part of digestion or lymph drainage.

items.prompt: Why does your breathing rate rise during vigorous exercise?

options.label: Blood loses all oxygen at once, so the heart signals the lungs to refill it immediately
Lungs shrink during exercise, so the body must breathe faster to fill the smaller space
Muscles make more carbon dioxide, and rising blood CO2 signals the brain to breathe faster
Air becomes thinner when moving, so the body breathes faster to take in more oxygen

rubric: Higher CO2 is detected and drives the brainstem to increase breathing rate.
Other options invent lung shrinkage or sudden oxygen loss that do not occur.

items.prompt: Which features help the small intestine absorb nutrients efficiently? Select all that apply.

options.label: Strong acid that absorbs nutrients directly
A rich blood supply carrying nutrients away
Villi that greatly increase surface area
Very thick walls that block diffusion

rubric: Villi increase surface area and blood flow carries absorbed nutrients away, maintaining the gradient.
Absorptive walls are thin, and strong acid is found in the stomach, not used for absorption.

items.prompt: A person stands up quickly from lying down and feels dizzy for a few seconds before it passes. A teacher asks you to explain what is going on in the body.

options.label: The heart stops briefly on standing, and the dizziness ends once the heart restarts by itself
Lungs take in too much oxygen on standing, and dizziness ends once breathing slows down
Blood pools in the legs, lowering flow to the brain until reflexes raise heart rate and constrict vessels
Bones press on nerves when upright, and the dizziness ends once the muscles relax again

rubric: Gravity pools blood in the legs, briefly reducing brain perfusion until the baroreceptor reflex corrects it.
The distractors give causes that do not occur in normal standing.

items.prompt: Why are the walls of the alveoli only one cell thick?

options.label: So the lungs can push air along by contracting their own muscle
So mucus can move freely through the walls to trap dust
So the alveoli can store extra air between breaths for later use
So oxygen and carbon dioxide can diffuse quickly between air and blood

rubric: Thin walls beside capillaries shorten the diffusion distance for gas exchange.
Lungs have no muscle in the alveoli; breathing is driven by the diaphragm and rib muscles.

items.prompt: Which situation is an example of negative feedback in homeostasis?

options.label: Nerve membrane depolarises and opens more sodium channels, which depolarises further
Body temperature rises and sweating starts, which cools the body back down
Contractions during labour cause release of more oxytocin, which strengthens contractions
A clot forms and attracts more platelets, which enlarges the clot

rubric: Negative feedback reverses a change and returns the variable toward its set point.
The other options are positive feedback, which amplifies the original change.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes arteries from veins?

options.label: Arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood and veins always carry oxygen-poor blood
Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry blood back toward it
Arteries have valves to stop backflow and veins have thick muscular walls
Veins carry blood away from the heart and arteries carry blood toward it

rubric: Arteries and veins are defined by direction of flow relative to the heart.
The pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood, so the oxygen-content rule fails.

items.prompt: What is the main effect of insulin on blood glucose?

options.label: It slows digestion so less glucose is absorbed from the gut
It helps cells take up glucose, lowering the level in the blood
It converts fat directly into glucose, raising the level in the blood
It signals the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose

rubric: Insulin promotes glucose uptake by cells and storage as glycogen, lowering blood glucose.
The first option describes glucagon, a common mix-up.

items.prompt: What is the role of a sensory (afferent) neuron?

options.label: It produces hormones that travel in the blood to target organs
It connects other neurons inside the spinal cord only
It carries commands from the brain to muscles so they contract
It carries impulses from receptors toward the central nervous system

rubric: Afferent neurons conduct information from receptors toward the CNS.
Motor neurons carry commands out to effectors, which is the most common confusion.

items.prompt: Which of the following are functions of the kidneys? Select all that apply.

options.label: Filtering waste products such as urea from the blood
Helping regulate water and electrolyte balance
Storing bile for fat digestion
Releasing renin, which helps control blood pressure
Producing insulin to control blood glucose

rubric: Kidneys filter wastes, balance fluids and electrolytes, and release renin.
Insulin comes from the pancreas and bile is stored in the gallbladder.

items.prompt: A student stands up very quickly after lying down and feels briefly dizzy. A few seconds later the feeling passes. Which explanation best accounts for this?

options.label: Blood thickens when a person stands, so the heart cannot pump it until the kidneys thin it
Gravity pools blood in the legs, lowering blood return and brain flow until reflexes raise heart rate and vessel tone
The brain briefly stops receiving oxygen because the lungs pause gas exchange when posture changes
The skeletal muscles of the legs release hormones that block blood flow to the head for a short time

rubric: Standing causes pooling; baroreceptor reflexes quickly restore blood pressure.
Other options invent respiratory, blood-viscosity or muscle-hormone mechanisms that do not occur.

items.prompt: A resting adult has a heart rate of 70 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 70 mL per beat. What is the cardiac output?

options.label: 140 mL/min
4,900 mL/min
49,000 mL/min
1,400 mL/min

rubric: Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume = 70 x 70 = 4,900 mL/min.
Other values come from misplaced decimal places or wrong operations.

items.prompt: Oxygenated blood has just left the lungs. Through which structure does it travel to reach the left atrium?

options.label: The pulmonary artery
The vena cava
The pulmonary veins
The aorta

rubric: Pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
The pulmonary artery is a common wrong pick because of its name linking to the lungs.

items.prompt: A person touches a hot pan and pulls their hand away before feeling pain. In the spinal cord, which step comes immediately after the sensory neuron fires?

options.label: The signal passes straight to the skin receptors that detected the heat
The signal triggers the adrenal glands to release hormones into the blood
The signal goes up to the cerebral cortex, which then orders the withdrawal
The signal is processed by an interneuron, which activates a motor neuron

rubric: In a reflex arc, integration in the spinal cord links sensory input to a motor neuron.
Pain awareness comes from the brain after the withdrawal has begun.

items.prompt: A weightlifter lifts a dumbbell by bending the elbow, with the biceps as the agonist. What happens to the triceps during this movement?

options.label: It detaches from the bone until the arm is lowered
It contracts equally to keep the elbow from bending too far
It relaxes and lengthens as the antagonist
It contracts and shortens to help the biceps

rubric: Antagonist muscles relax to allow the agonist to produce movement.
Co-contraction at equal strength would prevent the elbow from flexing.

items.prompt: A person has not eaten for 12 hours and blood glucose begins to fall. Which response should you expect?

options.label: Adrenal glands stop releasing all hormones to save energy
The pancreas converts muscle protein directly into insulin
Glucagon rises and the liver releases glucose from glycogen
Insulin rises so cells take up more glucose from the blood

rubric: Falling glucose triggers glucagon, which prompts glycogen breakdown in the liver.
Insulin would lower glucose further, so it is the wrong direction.

items.prompt: A person starts running hard. Which changes would you expect in the body? Select all that apply.

options.label: Blood flow to the digestive tract increases
Heart rate and stroke volume increase
Body core temperature drops sharply
Blood flow to working skeletal muscle increases
Bronchioles widen and breathing becomes deeper

rubric: Exercise raises cardiac output, ventilation and blood flow to working muscle.
Blood is diverted away from the gut, and heat production raises temperature.

items.prompt: A volunteer breathes in and out of a small paper bag for a minute. The air in the bag becomes richer in carbon dioxide. What should you predict about the volunteer's breathing, and why?

options.label: Breathing rate rises because chemoreceptors detect higher CO2 and acidity in the blood
Breathing stays the same because only oxygen levels control the breathing centre
Breathing slows because extra carbon dioxide relaxes the diaphragm
Breathing stops briefly because oxygen levels in the blood become too high

rubric: Rising CO2 lowers blood pH, and chemoreceptors drive the brainstem to increase ventilation.
The last option reverses the main driver, which is CO2 rather than oxygen.

items.prompt: At rest a person has a heart rate of 75 beats/min and a stroke volume of 70 mL. During a bleed, heart rate rises to 100 beats/min and stroke volume falls to 50 mL. What is the new cardiac output?

options.label: 3.5 L/min
7.0 L/min
5.0 L/min
5.25 L/min

rubric: Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume = 100 x 50 = 5000 mL/min.
5.25 L/min is the resting value; learners assume a higher heart rate always raises output.

items.prompt: A patient's blood pressure is 130/85 mmHg. Using mean arterial pressure = diastolic + one third of pulse pressure, what is the MAP?

options.label: 107 mmHg
85 mmHg
100 mmHg
115 mmHg

rubric: Pulse pressure is 45; one third is 15; MAP = 85 + 15 = 100 mmHg.
107 comes from simply averaging systolic and diastolic, ignoring that diastole lasts longer than systole.

items.prompt: A resting adult has a tidal volume of 500 mL, anatomical dead space of 150 mL and a respiratory rate of 12 breaths/min. What is the alveolar ventilation?

options.label: 5400 mL/min
1800 mL/min
4200 mL/min
6000 mL/min

rubric: Alveolar ventilation = (500 - 150) x 12 = 4200 mL/min.
6000 mL/min is minute ventilation, which ignores dead space that does not exchange gas.

items.prompt: A patient is given a drug that selectively blocks beta-1 adrenergic receptors in the heart. Which change would you predict in the heart?

options.label: Heart rate falls and contraction force rises because filling time increases
Heart rate and contraction force are unchanged because beta-2 receptors compensate
Heart rate falls and contraction force falls because sympathetic input is blunted
Heart rate rises and contraction force falls because the vagus dominates

rubric: Beta-1 receptors mediate sympathetic stimulation of rate and contractility, so blocking them lowers both.
The distractors misassign vagal dominance or assume beta-2 receptors take over in the heart.

items.prompt: A person with type 1 diabetes skips their insulin dose and eats a carbohydrate meal. Which change in blood glucose and cause would you predict?

options.label: It rises because glucagon is suppressed and the pancreas releases more
It rises because muscle and fat cells take up less glucose
It stays stable because glucose uptake in cells is insulin independent
It falls because the liver stores more glucose as glycogen

rubric: Without insulin, GLUT4-mediated uptake in muscle and fat falls, so glucose stays high after a meal.
Distractors reverse insulin's actions or claim uptake needs no insulin.

items.prompt: A healthy person stands up abruptly from lying down and arterial pressure at the carotid sinus briefly drops. Which responses of the baroreceptor reflex would you expect? Select all that apply.

options.label: Constriction of systemic arterioles
Increased sympathetic outflow to the heart
Increased vagal (parasympathetic) tone to the heart
Increased heart rate

rubric: Lowered baroreceptor firing raises sympathetic output, causing tachycardia and vasoconstriction to restore pressure.
Increased vagal tone would slow the heart and worsen the pressure drop.

items.prompt: A hiker sweats heavily on a hot day and loses about 2 L of fluid without drinking any water. Plasma osmolality rises. Using what you know about fluid balance, what would you predict about the hormone response and urine?

options.label: Aldosterone release falls, producing large volumes of salty urine
ADH release rises, producing a small volume of concentrated urine
ANP release rises, producing a small volume of concentrated urine
ADH release falls, producing large volumes of dilute urine

rubric: Raised osmolality stimulates hypothalamic osmoreceptors, increasing ADH and water reabsorption in the collecting ducts.
Distractors reverse the direction of ADH or choose ANP, which promotes sodium and water loss.

items.prompt: A patient has arterial blood pH 7.28, PaCO2 60 mmHg and a near-normal bicarbonate. Which cause best explains this picture?

options.label: Prolonged vomiting that loses gastric hydrochloric acid
Opioid overdose that depresses the brainstem respiratory centre
Anxiety-driven hyperventilation that blows off carbon dioxide
Diabetic ketoacidosis that adds ketoacids to the blood

rubric: Low pH with high PaCO2 indicates respiratory acidosis, from hypoventilation such as opioid-induced depression.
The other options produce respiratory alkalosis, metabolic alkalosis or metabolic acidosis.

items.prompt: Blood tests show high TSH and low free T4. Using the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid feedback loop, where is the most likely fault?

options.label: The target tissues, which are removing T4 from blood too fast
The pituitary, which is failing to secrete enough TSH
The hypothalamus, which is secreting too much TRH
The thyroid gland, which cannot respond to the TSH it receives

rubric: Low T4 removes negative feedback so the pituitary raises TSH; the gland itself is failing (primary hypothyroidism).
A pituitary fault would give low TSH, not high.

items.prompt: After a stroke, a patient has weakness of the right arm and leg and a drooping right lower face. Which explanation best accounts for the side of the weakness?

options.label: Damage to the right cerebellum, since it controls muscle strength on its own side
Damage to the right motor cortex, since fibres stay on the same side
Damage to the left motor cortex, since most corticospinal fibres cross in the medulla
Damage to the left spinal cord, since sensory fibres cross at the brainstem

rubric: Most corticospinal fibres decussate at the medullary pyramids, so a left cortical lesion causes right weakness.
Distractors ignore decussation or confuse cerebellar coordination with motor strength.

items.prompt: A patient has swollen ankles, distended neck veins and clear lungs on auscultation. Which mechanism best explains the ankle swelling?

options.label: Failure of the right ventricle raises systemic venous hydrostatic pressure
Failure of the left ventricle raises pulmonary capillary pressure
Loss of plasma albumin from the liver lowers capillary oncotic pressure
Blocked lymphatic drainage from the legs prevents return of fluid

rubric: Distended neck veins with clear lungs point to right-sided failure, backing blood up into systemic veins and pushing fluid out of capillaries.
Left failure would produce pulmonary congestion; albumin loss and lymphatic block would not explain the neck veins.

items.prompt: A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease has a low red cell count but normal iron stores and vitamin B12. Which is the most likely cause of the anaemia?

options.label: Overproduction of hepcidin by the bone marrow
Reduced erythropoietin production by damaged kidneys
Reduced oxygen levels in tissue suppressing stem cells
Excess destruction of red cells in the spleen

rubric: Kidneys are the main source of erythropoietin, so damaged kidneys cause under-stimulated red cell production.
Low oxygen would normally raise erythropoietin, so that distractor reverses the physiology.

items.prompt: In emphysema, forced expiration becomes difficult and air is trapped in the lungs. Which findings help explain this? Select all that apply.

options.label: Small airways collapse early because they lose radial traction
Weakened diaphragm nerves prevent any inspiration
Excess surfactant raises surface tension in the alveoli
Destruction of alveolar walls reduces elastic recoil

rubric: Loss of elastic tissue lowers recoil and lets small airways collapse on expiration, trapping air.
Excess surfactant is not a feature, and emphysema does not involve phrenic nerve failure.

items.prompt: A patient has moon-shaped facies, easy bruising and a high blood pressure. Tests show high plasma cortisol and a very low ACTH. Which diagnosis best fits, given how the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis works?

options.label: A pituitary adenoma secreting excess ACTH
An adrenal tumour secreting cortisol independently of ACTH
An ectopic lung tumour secreting excess ACTH
Adrenal failure with reduced cortisol feedback to the pituitary

rubric: High cortisol suppresses ACTH through negative feedback, so low ACTH means the cortisol source is autonomous, such as an adrenal tumour.
The ACTH-secreting tumours would give high ACTH, and adrenal failure would give low cortisol.

items.prompt: A patient with long-standing COPD has arterial PCO2 of 60 mmHg, raised bicarbonate and pH 7.37. Which process best explains the near-normal pH?

options.label: Hemoglobin released extra H+ in the lungs, neutralising carbonic acid
The liver converted lactate to bicarbonate faster during hypercapnia
Chemoreceptors drove ventilation up until PCO2 returned to normal
Kidneys retained bicarbonate over days, buffering the pH fall from CO2

rubric: Chronic CO2 retention is met by renal bicarbonate retention over days, which brings pH back toward normal.
Distractors ignore that PCO2 is still high or credit fast mechanisms (chemoreceptors, hemoglobin) for a slow compensation.

items.prompt: An older adult on a high-dose loop diuretic becomes dizzy on standing. Which analysis best explains this?

options.label: Fluid loss raises blood viscosity, which slows flow to the brain when upright
Low blood volume cuts venous return, so the baroreflex cannot restore output in time
Potassium loss paralyses vascular smooth muscle, so veins cannot constrict
Diuretics block carotid baroreceptors, so heart rate cannot rise on standing

rubric: Reduced plasma volume lowers venous return and stroke volume on standing, and the baroreflex cannot fully compensate.
Distractors invent receptor blockade or viscosity effects rather than the volume-preload mechanism.

items.prompt: A knife wound hemisects the right side of the spinal cord at T10. Which pattern of deficits is expected below the lesion?

options.label: Left leg weakness and loss of vibration, right leg loss of pain and temperature
Right leg weakness with loss of pain and temperature in the right leg too
Equal loss of all sensation and movement in both legs
Right leg weakness and loss of vibration, left leg loss of pain and temperature

rubric: Motor and dorsal column tracts are uncrossed at this level, while spinothalamic fibres have already crossed, giving ipsilateral motor and vibration loss and contralateral pain and temperature loss.
Distractors swap the sides or ignore the different crossing points of the tracts.

items.prompt: A pulmonary embolus blocks blood flow to one lung segment while its airways stay open. How does that segment's ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) ratio change, and why?

options.label: V/Q rises, because air still enters alveoli that get little or no blood
V/Q is unchanged, because ventilation and perfusion adjust together at once
V/Q falls, because blocked vessels trap air inside the alveoli
V/Q falls, because alveoli collapse as soon as blood flow stops

rubric: With ventilation preserved and perfusion lost, V/Q rises toward infinity, which is alveolar dead space.
Distractors confuse the direction of the ratio or assume instant matching of ventilation to flow.

items.prompt: A patient has high TSH, low free T4 and a goitre. Where is the fault most likely located?

options.label: In the adrenal cortex, whose cortisol deficit lowers T4 release and raises TSH
In the hypothalamus, which has stopped releasing TRH, so thyroid output falls
In the thyroid gland, which cannot respond to TSH, so feedback inhibition is lost
In the pituitary, which secretes TSH autonomously and drives T4 upward

rubric: High TSH with low T4 means the pituitary is responding normally and the thyroid is failing (primary hypothyroidism).
Distractors place the fault upstream, which would give low or high TSH patterns that do not match.

items.prompt: A patient has severe aortic valve stenosis. Which findings follow from the increased afterload on the left ventricle? Select all that apply.

options.label: Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy develops over time
Systolic pressure in the ventricle exceeds aortic pressure by a large gradient
Left ventricular wall thinning develops as the first adaptation
Coronary perfusion improves as the ventricle contracts harder
Stroke volume cannot rise much during exertion

rubric: Pressure overload thickens the wall, creates a systolic gradient across the valve, and fixes outflow during exercise.
Wall thinning and improved coronary perfusion reverse the real effects; hypertrophy raises oxygen demand and can impair perfusion.

items.prompt: A 28-year-old marathon runner drank several litres of plain water during the race and collapses, confused. Serum sodium is 124 mmol/L. Which analysis best explains the low sodium?

options.label: Aldosterone excess drove urinary sodium loss faster than the sweat losses
Water intake exceeded losses while ADH stayed high, so plasma sodium was diluted
Sweat lost more water than sodium, so the remaining plasma sodium became concentrated
Sodium was trapped inside muscle cells after exertion, with body water normal

rubric: Exercise-associated hyponatremia comes from excess water relative to sodium, with persistent nonosmotic ADH limiting water excretion.
The sweat-loss distractor would predict raised sodium; the others invent sodium shifts not typical of this picture.

items.prompt: A clinic needs a routine marker of glomerular filtration that is freely filtered, barely reabsorbed, and little affected by hydration or protein intake. Which marker best meets these criteria?

options.label: Urine output per hour, since filtration volume sets urine volume directly
Blood urea nitrogen, since urea is filtered and reflects nephron function
Serum creatinine used to estimate GFR, since it is filtered and little reabsorbed
Urine specific gravity, since it reflects how well the kidney clears solutes

rubric: Creatinine is filtered, minimally reabsorbed and fairly steady, so it fits the criteria.
BUN varies with protein intake and hydration; urine output and specific gravity reflect concentrating, not filtration.

items.prompt: A student claims: 'Hemoglobin saturation falls in direct proportion to PO2, so a drop from 100 to 80 mmHg should cut saturation by about a fifth.' Which critique is best?

options.label: The curve is linear, but its slope depends on temperature and pH only
Saturation rises as PO2 falls because affinity for oxygen increases
The curve is sigmoidal and flat at high PO2, so that drop changes saturation only slightly
Saturation depends on hemoglobin concentration, so PO2 changes have no effect

rubric: The oxygen dissociation curve plateaus above about 60 mmHg, so modest PO2 falls there barely change saturation.
Distractors claim linearity, reverse the relationship, or confuse saturation with oxygen content.

items.prompt: On a monitored ward, which finding poses the greatest immediate threat to cerebral perfusion and should be treated first?

options.label: Sinus bradycardia at 52 in a trained athlete, because the rate is below 60
Atrial fibrillation at 90 beats/min, because atria lose coordinated contraction
First-degree AV block, because conduction is delayed through the node
Ventricular fibrillation, because the ventricles quiver without ejecting blood

rubric: Ventricular fibrillation abolishes cardiac output at once, so brain perfusion stops within seconds.
The other rhythms usually maintain output; the distractors rely on rate or conduction numbers without judging haemodynamic effect.

items.prompt: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has pH 7.10, low bicarbonate, PCO2 22 mmHg, and deep rapid breathing. Which judgment about the breathing is best supported?

options.label: It is primary hyperventilation from anxiety, since low PCO2 shows alkalosis
It is harmful overcompensation, since low PCO2 pushes pH further down
It is a sign of lung failure, since hypoxia drives deep breaths
It is appropriate compensation, since blowing off CO2 raises pH toward normal

rubric: Low pH with low bicarbonate is metabolic acidosis; low PCO2 shows respiratory compensation that limits the pH fall.
Distractors misread low PCO2 as the primary problem or as damaging, ignoring the acidaemia.

items.prompt: A postmenopausal woman wants to slow bone loss without drugs. Criteria: the plan must address both bone-forming stimulus and mineral supply. Which plan is best justified?

options.label: Weight-bearing resistance exercise with calcium and vitamin D, because load stimulates osteoblasts and minerals supply them
Swimming daily, because buoyancy protects joints and still loads the skeleton
Vitamin D alone, because it directly builds bone matrix without any need for load
High-dose calcium alone, because mineral intake is the only limit on bone density

rubric: Mechanical loading stimulates bone formation while calcium and vitamin D supply mineral and absorption, meeting both criteria.
Single-factor plans miss one criterion; swimming gives little skeletal loading.

items.prompt: Which are well-justified criticisms of using resting heart rate alone to judge a person's cardiac output? Select all that apply.

options.label: Caffeine, stress and dehydration shift resting rate without changing fitness
Beta-blockers lower rate regardless of the heart's pumping capacity
Rate is set only by the vagus nerve, so sympathetic input is irrelevant
Stroke volume differs between people, so equal rates may give different output
Heart rate cannot change with training, so it carries no information

rubric: Cardiac output is rate times stroke volume, and resting rate is influenced by many factors unrelated to pumping capacity.
The other options are false: training lowers resting rate, and both sympathetic and vagal input set rate.

items.prompt: A trauma patient has lost about 1.5 L of blood and is hypotensive. Staff must choose an IV fluid that expands plasma volume quickly and stays largely in the extracellular space. Which fluid is best justified?

options.label: 0.9% saline, because it is isotonic and stays in extracellular fluid
Sterile water, because it is the purest and moves rapidly into the blood
5% dextrose in water, because dextrose holds the water inside the vessels
0.45% saline, because it is hypotonic so it draws water into the vessels

rubric: Isotonic saline distributes across extracellular fluid, so it expands plasma without shifting water into cells.
Dextrose in water and hypotonic fluids distribute into all compartments and expand plasma poorly; sterile water would cause hemolysis.

items.prompt: A student argues that because hemoglobin is about 98% saturated at a PaO2 of 100 mmHg, giving a healthy person 100% oxygen will greatly raise tissue oxygen delivery. Which critique is best?

options.label: Oxygen delivery depends only on cardiac output, so arterial oxygen content has no effect on it
Hemoglobin is nearly full already, so only a small extra amount of dissolved oxygen is added
High oxygen sharply raises 2,3-BPG, shifting the curve left so hemoglobin releases less oxygen
Excess oxygen cannot bind hemoglobin, so the kidneys excrete it and blood content never rises

rubric: Near-saturated hemoglobin gains little; only dissolved O2 (about 0.003 mL/dL per mmHg) is added.
Distractors misstate oxygen transport: delivery is cardiac output times arterial content, and 2,3-BPG does not rise sharply with hyperoxia.

items.prompt: A clinician must judge which thyroid lab pattern best supports a central (pituitary or hypothalamic) cause of hypothyroidism rather than a primary thyroid cause. Which pattern does so?

options.label: Low free T4 with low or inappropriately normal TSH
High free T4 together with a suppressed TSH level now
Normal free T4 together with a mildly raised TSH level
Low free T4 together with a markedly raised TSH level

rubric: Without negative feedback working normally, low T4 with non-elevated TSH indicates failure above the thyroid.
High TSH with low T4 is primary failure; normal T4 with high TSH is subclinical primary disease; high T4 with low TSH is thyrotoxicosis.

items.prompt: A teaching note says high-flow oxygen worsens CO2 retention in COPD solely by removing the hypoxic respiratory drive. Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: Wrong: oxygen directly dilates the airways, so any retention comes from mucus plugging after treatment starts
Wrong: oxygen lowers cellular CO2 production, so any retention must come from sedation and not from the oxygen
Correct: peripheral chemoreceptors are the only input to breathing, so removing hypoxia stops ventilation entirely
Incomplete: worse V/Q mismatch from lost hypoxic vasoconstriction and the Haldane effect also raise PaCO2

rubric: Hypoxic drive loss is only part of the story; V/Q mismatch and the Haldane effect contribute substantially.
Distractors either overstate the drive explanation or invent unrelated mechanisms.

items.prompt: A patient passes 8 L of dilute urine daily and urine stays dilute after water deprivation. Judging by what discriminates central from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, which result after desmopressin best supports a central cause?

options.label: Urine osmolality rises substantially, showing the collecting ducts still respond to ADH
Plasma sodium falls sharply, showing excess ADH secretion from the posterior pituitary
Urine volume doubles, showing desmopressin downregulates aquaporin channels in the ducts
Urine stays dilute, showing the kidney is unresponsive to ADH although release is normal

rubric: A response to exogenous ADH shows the kidney works and the hormone is lacking.
Persistent dilute urine indicates nephrogenic DI; the other options misdescribe desmopressin's action.

items.prompt: A patient with severe fixed aortic stenosis needs blood pressure lowered. Judging by hemodynamic risk, why is a potent arteriolar vasodilator the most hazardous choice?

options.label: It causes reflex bradycardia that lengthens diastole and overfills the hypertrophied ventricle
Output cannot rise through the fixed valve, so falling resistance drops pressure and coronary perfusion
It raises venous return sharply, so preload overload causes pulmonary oedema within minutes
It raises afterload across the valve, so wall stress climbs and the ventricle cannot eject blood

rubric: With fixed obstruction, cardiac output cannot compensate for lower SVR, so hypotension and coronary hypoperfusion follow.
Vasodilators lower, not raise, afterload and typically cause reflex tachycardia.

items.prompt: A reviewer checks a case summary of advanced chronic kidney disease. Which statements about its anemia and mineral-bone disorder are physiologically sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: Reduced phosphate filtration causes retention, which stimulates parathyroid hormone and FGF23 release
Excess renal aldosterone production drives bone resorption and lowers the red cell count
Loss of renal intrinsic factor causes B12 deficiency and a macrocytic anemia in these patients
Damaged peritubular interstitial cells make less erythropoietin, so red cell production falls
Reduced 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity lowers active vitamin D, which impairs calcium absorption

rubric: Low EPO, low calcitriol and phosphate retention are the core mechanisms.
Intrinsic factor comes from gastric parietal cells, and aldosterone excess is not the cause of CKD anemia or bone disease.

items.prompt: A marathon runner who drank water at every aid station collapses, confused, with serum sodium 124 mmol/L, weight above her starting weight and no signs of dehydration. Her ADH is high despite low plasma osmolality. Which judgement best guides her care?

options.label: Sweat sodium loss alone caused it, so large volumes of plain water will correct the sodium level
Aldosterone deficiency is wasting sodium in the urine, so fluid restriction would worsen her picture
Dilutional hyponatraemia from intake exceeding excretion with non-osmotic ADH; avoid more hypotonic fluid
Dehydration triggered the ADH release, so rapid litres of isotonic fluid are needed to restore weight

rubric: Weight gain and high ADH with low osmolality indicate water excess with non-osmotic ADH, so more free water is harmful.
Distractors assume dehydration or pure sodium loss, ignoring the weight gain and inappropriate ADH.

items.prompt: You must test whether the ventilatory rise on arrival at altitude is driven mainly by peripheral chemoreceptors, using only a brief, noninvasive manipulation. Which design best fits?

options.label: Give 5% CO2 in air and record the ventilation rise to estimate hypoxic chemoreceptor activity
Have the subject hold their breath and time the break point as a measure of central CO2 sensitivity
Briefly switch the subject to 100% oxygen and watch for an abrupt fall in ventilation
Measure resting heart rate over 24 hours to infer the strength of carotid body signalling

rubric: Brief hyperoxia removes the hypoxic stimulus to carotid bodies, so an abrupt fall shows their contribution.
CO2 breathing and breath-holding probe CO2 sensitivity, and heart rate does not isolate carotid body drive.

items.prompt: Design a rehydration fluid for a child with secretory diarrhoea who can drink. Constraints: no IV access, it must use a gut transport process that stays intact, and it must not add osmotic water loss.

options.label: Clean water with sodium chloride only, because sodium alone is absorbed by an unimpaired transporter
Clean water with a high glucose concentration, to supply energy and draw water in by osmosis alone
Clean water with sodium and glucose in similar molar amounts so SGLT1 co-transport draws water in
Clean water with potassium and bicarbonate only, to replace the electrolytes that were lost in stool

rubric: Sodium-glucose co-transport via SGLT1 stays intact in secretory diarrhoea, and balanced concentrations avoid osmotic loss.
High glucose is hyperosmolar and worsens losses; sodium alone lacks the coupled carrier route.

items.prompt: Design an insulin plan for a person with type 1 diabetes about to do 60 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise soon after a meal. Constraints: avoid hypoglycaemia from contraction-driven glucose uptake, and avoid ketosis.

options.label: Keep basal insulin, reduce the mealtime dose beforehand, and have fast-acting carbohydrate ready
Leave all doses unchanged and rely on the liver to release enough glucose throughout exercise
Raise the mealtime dose so insulin peaks during exercise and offsets the stress hormone rise
Stop basal insulin during exercise, since contracting muscle takes up glucose without any insulin

rubric: Basal insulin prevents ketosis while a reduced bolus counters exercise-enhanced uptake and sensitivity.
Stopping basal risks ketosis, raising the bolus risks hypoglycaemia, and the liver alone cannot offset peak insulin.

items.prompt: A learner's negative-feedback diagram for heat stress contains skin and core thermoreceptors, a hypothalamic set-point comparator and sweat glands. Which missing element would most complete the cooling response?

options.label: Thyroid hormone release to boost basal metabolic rate and so dissipate more body heat
Posterior pituitary ADH raising urine output so that excess body heat is shed in urine
Skin arterioles dilating through reduced sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone, increasing heat loss
Skeletal muscle shivering to raise heat production back toward the set point value

rubric: Cutaneous vasodilation is the key effector that increases heat loss alongside sweating.
The other options raise heat production or are unrelated to heat loss.

items.prompt: Design the minimal bedside data set to separate cardiogenic, hypovolaemic and distributive shock in a hypotensive patient. Which set best meets this requirement?

options.label: Urine output and capillary refill, since both are normal in two types and low in only one
Haemoglobin, glucose and lactate, since each shock type produces a distinct pattern in them
Cardiac output, systemic vascular resistance and a filling-pressure estimate such as JVP or CVP
Heart rate, temperature and respiratory rate, which together define the shock category involved

rubric: Output, resistance and preload together separate pump failure, volume loss and vasodilation.
Vital signs, lactate and perfusion signs are nonspecific and overlap across shock types.

items.prompt: You are building a simulation of the seconds-scale orthostatic response on standing. Which elements must the model include? Select all that apply.

options.label: Thyroid hormone secretion that raises cardiac output within seconds of standing
Medullary integration that raises sympathetic output and lowers vagal output
Carotid and aortic baroreceptor afferents that fire less as arterial pressure falls
Aldosterone-driven renal sodium reabsorption as the main early restorer of pressure
Effectors that raise heart rate and contractility and constrict veins and arterioles

rubric: The baroreflex arc needs sensors, a medullary integrator and autonomic effectors.
Aldosterone and thyroid hormone act over hours to days, not seconds.

items.prompt: A man with a T4 spinal cord injury develops a pounding headache, flushing above the injury, BP 210/120 and HR 52 after his catheter kinks. No drugs are available yet. Which immediate plan best fits the mechanism?

options.label: Lay him flat with his legs raised to improve venous return, then wait for pressure to settle
Give a rapid fluid bolus to raise the heart rate, then recheck once the pulse is normal
Sit him upright, loosen tight clothing and relieve the bladder trigger by clearing the catheter
Apply ice to the legs to constrict vessels below the injury and so lower the blood pressure

rubric: Autonomic dysreflexia is driven by a noxious stimulus below the lesion; sitting up lowers BP and removing the trigger stops the reflex.
Lying flat, fluids or cold stimuli worsen hypertension or add triggers.
